# Linear Models {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Classes of Linear Models {.smaller}

| Abbreviation       | Name                       | Description                  |
|:------------------|:-------------------------|:---------------------------|
| **GLM**            | General Linear Model       | Continuous variables         |
| **GLMM**           | General Linear Mixed Model | Mixed continuous/categorical |
| **Generalized LM** | Generalized Linear Model   | Non-normal response          |
| **GAM**            | Generalized Additive Model | Non-linear relationships     |


## What is a Ordinary Linear Model?

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i$$

-   $\beta_0$: intercept
-   $\beta_1$: slope
-   $\epsilon_i$: error/residual


## Simple Linear Regression Example {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-example-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

# This part of the code creates two variables, one with random error that is normally distributed
set.seed(123)
x <- runif(50, 0, 10)
y <- 2 + 1.5*x + rnorm(50, 0, 2)

# This part of the code is fitting the model, plotting the points and the best fit line
my_lm <- lm(y ~ x)
plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
abline(my_lm, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

## Linear Regression Example Code {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-example-code
```

## Hypothesis Tests in Regression {.smaller}

![](images/week05_28_reduced_vs_full_model_residuals.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}


## Hypothesis Tests in Regression {.smaller}

$$H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \quad \text{(no relationship)}$$ $$H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0 \quad \text{(relationship exists)}$$

Compares:

-   Reduced model: $y_i = \beta_0 + \epsilon_i$
-   Full model: $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i$



## Sum of Squares

| Term         | Description                    |
|:-------------|:-------------------------------|
| $SS_{Total}$ | Total variability in data      |
| $SS_{Model}$ | Variability explained by model |
| $SS_{Error}$ | Unexplained variability        |

$$SS_{Total} = SS_{Model} + SS_{Error}$$


## Hypothesis Tests in Regression {.smaller}

![](images/week05_29_f_ratio_f_distribution_hypothesis.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}


## R² as Measure of Fit (~ effect size)

$$R^2 = \frac{SS_{Model}}{SS_{Total}} = 1 - \frac{SS_{Error}}{SS_{Total}}$$



$R^2$ is the proportion of variance in Y explained by X.

## Components of an lm Object {.smaller}

When you fit a model with `lm()`, R stores many useful components in the returned object:

| Component | Description | Accessor Function |
|:------------------|:---------------------|:-------------------------------|
| `coefficients` | Estimated $\beta$ values | `coef()` |
| `residuals` | Observed minus fitted values ($y_i - \hat{y}_i$) | `residuals()` or `resid()` |
| `fitted.values` | Predicted values ($\hat{y}_i$) | `fitted()` |
| `rank` | Rank of the design matrix | — |
| `df.residual` | Residual degrees of freedom | `df.residual()` |
| `call` | The original function call | — |
| `terms` | The model formula terms | — |
| `model` | The data frame used for fitting | `model.frame()` |
| `qr` | QR decomposition of design matrix | — |
| `effects` | Orthogonal effects | — |

## Extracting Model Information {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-extract-1

```

# Subgroups in simple linear regression

## Simpson's Paradox {.smaller}

A trend that appears in groups can disappear or reverse when groups are combined.

![](images/week05_14_simpsons_paradox_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Simpson's Paradox Explained {.smaller}

![](images/week05_15_simpsons_paradox_explained_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## In-Class Demo: Simpson's Paradox with Iris Data {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: simpsons-paradox-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Overall: negative correlation
plot(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length, pch = 19, col = "gray50",
     xlab = "Sepal Width", ylab = "Sepal Length",
     main = "All Species Combined")
abline(lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, iris), col = "black", lwd = 2)

# By species: positive correlation within each!
colors <- c("red", "green3", "blue")
plot(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length, pch = 19,
     col = colors[as.numeric(iris$Species)],
     xlab = "Sepal Width", ylab = "Sepal Length",
     main = "By Species: Direction Reverses!")
for(i in 1:3) {
  sp_data <- iris[iris$Species == levels(iris$Species)[i], ]
  abline(lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, sp_data), col = colors[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", levels(iris$Species), col = colors, pch = 19, cex = 0.8)
```

## Simpson's Paradox Code {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: simpsons-paradox-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Overall: negative correlation
plot(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length, pch = 19, col = "gray50",
     xlab = "Sepal Width", ylab = "Sepal Length",
     main = "All Species Combined")
abline(lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, iris), col = "black", lwd = 2)
cat("Overall correlation:", round(cor(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length), 3))

# By species: positive correlation within each!
colors <- c("red", "green3", "blue")
plot(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length, pch = 19,
     col = colors[as.numeric(iris$Species)],
     xlab = "Sepal Width", ylab = "Sepal Length",
     main = "By Species: Direction Reverses!")
for(i in 1:3) {
  sp_data <- iris[iris$Species == levels(iris$Species)[i], ]
  abline(lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, sp_data), col = colors[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", levels(iris$Species), col = colors, pch = 19, cex = 0.8)
```

::: callout-important
The overall negative trend reverses to positive within each species — a classic confounding variable problem!
:::

# Residual Analysis {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Assumptions of Linear Models {.smaller}

-   Independent errors (residuals)
-   Equal variance of residuals (homoscedasticity)
-   Normally-distributed residuals

::: callout-note
Robustness improves with large sample sizes and balanced designs.
:::

## Leverage and Influence {.smaller}

-   **Leverage**: How much of an outlier in x-space
-   **Residual**: How much of an outlier in y-space
-   **Cook's D**: Overall influence on fitted model

::: callout-warning
Cook's D ≥ 1 indicates highly influential observations.
:::

# Model I vs Model II Regression {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## When to Use Model II Regression {.smaller}

**Model I (OLS) Regression:**

-   Assumes predictor X is measured **without error**
-   Y contains all the measurement error
-   Standard `lm()` in R

**Model II Regression:**

-   Both X and Y have **measurement error**
-   Neither variable is controlled/fixed
-   Use when both variables are random measurements

::: callout-note
Use Model II when both X and Y are biological measurements (e.g., body size vs organ size, two gene expression levels).
:::

## Model II Regression Methods {.smaller}

| Method | Abbreviation | Description |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Major Axis** | MA | Minimizes perpendicular distances |
| **Standard Major Axis** | SMA | Geometric mean regression |
| **Ranged Major Axis** | RMA | Accounts for range differences |
| **Ordinary Least Squares** | OLS | Standard regression (for comparison) |


## Types of Linear Regression {.smaller}

Not all regression is created equal! The choice depends on **measurement error**:

![Model I (OLS) vs Model II regression types](images/week05_40_model_types_ols_ma_rma.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Regression Type Examples {.smaller}

![Comparison of OLS (Type I) and Type II regression methods](images/week05_41_regression_type_examples.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## When to Use Each Model Type {.smaller}

![Guidelines for choosing between OLS, MA, and RMA regression](images/week05_42_when_to_use_model_types.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}


## Model II Regression with lmodel2 {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(lmodel2)

# Model II regression when both X and Y have measurement error
# Example: comparing two measurement methods
mod2 <- lmodel2(Y ~ X, data = mydata, range.y = "relative", range.x = "relative")

# Returns OLS, MA, SMA (RMA), and ranged major axis results
summary(mod2)
plot(mod2)
```

::: callout-note
Use Model II regression when: - Both variables have measurement error - Neither variable is experimentally controlled - You're comparing methods or studying allometry
:::


## Model II Regression in R {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: model2-regression
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Install and load lmodel2 package
# install.packages("lmodel2")
library(lmodel2)

# Fit Model II regression
model2_result <- lmodel2(y ~ x, data = mydata)

# View results - provides OLS, MA, and SMA estimates
model2_result

# Plot with different regression lines
plot(mydata$x, mydata$y, pch = 19)
abline(model2_result$regression.results[2, 2],  # MA intercept
       model2_result$regression.results[2, 3],  # MA slope
       col = "blue", lty = 2)
abline(model2_result$regression.results[3, 2],  # SMA intercept
       model2_result$regression.results[3, 3],  # SMA slope
       col = "red", lty = 3)
```

## Choosing Between Model I and II {.smaller}

::: callout-tip
## Decision Guide

Use **Model I (OLS)** when:

-   X is controlled/manipulated experimentally
-   X is measured with negligible error
-   Goal is prediction of Y from X

Use **Model II (SMA/MA)** when:

-   Both variables are random biological measurements
-   Both have comparable measurement error
-   Goal is to describe the functional relationship
:::



# The Eugenics History of Statistics

## Galton's original data {.smaller}

![](images/week05_10_galton_regression_to_mean_height.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Galton as the Father of Eugenics

![](images/week6_Galton.jpeg){fig.align="center"}

-   Francis Galton: Darwin's half cousin
-   Studied human variation and genetic inheritance
    -   Human height, fingerprints, intelligence
    -   Correlation, regression toward the mean, and "nature versus nurture"
    -   Pioneered twin studies

## Galton as the Father of Eugenics

-   Believed that intelligence was hereditary based on surveying prominent academics in Europe
-   Used the ideas of **correlation** and **regression towards the mean** to argue that the upper class should breed amongst themselves to keep those "good genes" pure
-   Wanted to provide monetary incentives for "good" couples to marry and reproduce as a way to avoid the upper class being genetically muddied by the lower class

## A common sight at state fairs around the U.S. in the 1930s

-   Competitions for the "perfect family" to encourage public consciousness and support for eugenics

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width='50%', fig.asp=.75, fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/IMAGES2.013.jpeg")
```

## Galton, Charles Davenport & G. Stanley Hall

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width='50%', fig.asp=.75, fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/IMAGES2.014.jpeg")
```

## Logo of the US eugenics society

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width='80%', fig.asp=.75, fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/IMAGES2.015.jpeg")
```

-   American Eugenics Record Office (ERO) founded in Cold Springs Harbor

## Eugenics societies in America

-   Advocated for state laws to ban interracial marriages and promote sterilization of "unfit" individuals (negative eugenics) - especially black, Latinx, and Native American women
-   30 states passed laws to force mental institution patients to be sterilized
-   Between 1907 and 1963, over 64,000 individuals were forcibly sterilized under eugenic legislation in the United States

## RA Fisher and Eugenics in London

-   Developer of Fishers exact test, analysis of variance (ANOVA), null hypothesis, p values, maximum likelihood, probability density functions
-   Founding Chairman of the University of Cambridge Eugenics Society

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width='20%', fig.asp=.75, fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week6_fisher.jpeg")
```

## RA Fisher and Eugenics

-   1/3rd of his work "The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection" discussed eugenics and his theory that the fall of civilizations was due to the fertility of their upper classes being diminished
-   Used these statistical methods to test data on human variation to prove biological differences between human races
-   Eugenics and racism were the primary motivators for many of these statistical tests that we use today

## A direct line to Hitler and Nazism

-   Eugenics existed in America (and England) before it became popular in Germany.
-   By 1933, California had subjected more people to forceful sterilization than all other U.S. states combined.
-   The forced sterilization program engineered by the Nazis was partly inspired by California's.

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width='70%', fig.asp=.75, fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/IMAGES2.016.jpeg")
```

## Sterilizations continue in America

-   Our history books paint Nazi Germany as the primary evil of that time, while we try to cover up our significant role in eugenics
-   It wasn't until 1978 that the US passed regulations on sterilization procedures
-   California only passed a bill to outlaw sterilization of inmates in 2014
-   Certain members of the genetic engineering community threaten to bring back eugenics ideas
-   Our current President repeats eugenics talking points

## So, what do we do from here?

-   The statistical methods that Galton, Fisher, and others developed are useful science tools
-   Important to use these tools for good - improving our planet, human health, and technology
-   Important to acknowledge and not forget the history of science - educate others to avoid repeating history
